articles.headline_en: Meta restores PM Modi's Facebook video, says it was removed 'in error'
articles.significance: Shows how platform moderation affecting political leaders can quickly escalate into a state–platform confrontation, raising questions about error rates and political bias in automated enforcement systems.
articles.source: Moneycontrol (India) – included because Meta’s moderation and government pressure are directly relevant to European and global digital speech governance debates.
articles.summary_en: Moneycontrol reports that Meta briefly removed a Facebook video of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing young voters, triggering a formal summons from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to Meta’s global head of public policy.[1] Meta said the removal was the result of a technical glitch and restored the video, apologising and stating there was no violation of its community standards.[1] Indian officials reportedly sought an explanation and assurances against similar incidents affecting official government communications.[1]

editorial_overview: The available search results surfaced only one clearly relevant case, involving Meta’s temporary removal and restoration of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, which prompted government pressure and formal summoning of the company. While this incident is outside Europe, it illustrates dynamics that are central to current European debates: opaque platform moderation decisions, their impact on democratic political communication, and the willingness of governments to intervene. In the European context, similar controversies typically occur under the framework of the Digital Services Act and national hate-speech or disinformation laws, but no qualifying Europe-specific cases with adequate sourcing appeared in the last week in the retrieved results. The Modi–Meta dispute nonetheless underscores how quickly technical or moderation errors involving high-profile political figures can become diplomatic and regulatory issues, a pattern closely watched by European policymakers and regulators.
topic: Recent controversies over online political speech, moderation, and government pressure
